566459,ca.proc.d.1920-04-22.3.11.51,1920-04-22,1d093884-066e-4154-90c4-5125c80965b9,ca.m.5140,Mr. DOHERTY:,Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada,QUESTIONS.,BILL TO CONFIRM AGREEMENT WITH THE COMPANY.,,That remains in the

Pension Fund, in the Provident Fund. Those two funds, as annexed or connected associations of the Grand Trunk Railway Company continue to be annexed or connected institutions of the Grand Trunk Railway Company, which Grand Trunk Railway Company continues to own the railroad and to run it. What changes hands is the capital stock of the Grand Trunk Railway Company. I think, therefore, it must be abundantly clear that the question is, whether these men have a claim upon the Pension Fund or the Provident Fund. The Pension Fund and the Provident Fund will continue just as before; and if it should be ultimately decided that for any reason this money ought to be paid, it will properly be paid out of the Pension Fund, or the Provident Fund. I have not come here prepared to discuss the constitutions of these funds, but that is what I gathered from the observations of the hon. members to be the case. What then is the result?
In the first place, I have grave doubts whether this amendment is in order at
all, but I have no desire to insist on that-point; I refer to it merely for the purpose of pointing out how absolutely foreign this is to the Bill before the House. *

The Bill before the House has to do with a contract between this country and the Grand Trunk Railway Company and its sharehouders for the acquisition of its stock. What we are asked to do by the amendment is to declare that

Any right or interest of any employee of the Grand Trunk Railway Company existing in the pension system prior to the strike of the company's employees which occurred in July, 1910, is hereby declared not to have been affected by the said strike or any circumstance or condition arising out of or in connection therewith.

I have difficulty in conceiving how the connection is made as between this Bill and the present amendment, and I submit that for the consideration of the Speaker. In the meantime let me just ask the hon. gentleman: When he makes these frantic appeals to have, justice done at the last moment; asks us, in order to get at the result of what he considers justice, to proceed in the manner indicated at the outset^ namely, to determine the justice of this: claim, without the parties, without the-evidence, and above all, without one word on the part oLthe party that is to be condemned; does he not see that he is absolutely confusing what are the proper functions of Parliament in the way of doing justice with the functions that under the constitution and the law of this country belong to our courts? But, passing that over, does he not himself realize-I appeal to him for the last time-what a gross injustice would necessarily be involved in determining this case without hearing the party we are going to stand here and condemn? The hon. gentleman thinks it would be appalling if it should ever happen that the people of this country should pay those pensions. I said the other evening, and I say it again to-night, that I have not the slightest doubt that the people of this country would infinitely prefer to pay those pensions out of their own pockets to standing by and seeing this Parliament so far forget itself, so. far abuse its functions as to show itself to share the hon. gentleman's absolute incapacity for perceiving that the simplest justice requires that you hear a man or a company before you condemn, and to make the precedent that this Parliament will take upon itself to settle disputed claims ex parte, without any opportunity for discussion, throw it out to the world that everybody who thinks he has a grievance,-and of course, if the party is a

numerous body there will be more suspicion of its being able to exercise a political influence; that every person or number of men who believe themselves to have a claim -may come to Parliament to make their side of the case and Parliament will receive them with open arms, and if they have the good fortune to have an hon. gentleman sitting in this House who is convinced that he has personal knowledge of all the facts and is therefore competent to decide -though he was very close to being a party himself to the making of that agreement-will sit in judgment upon the case and pronounce who is wrong. Parliament in the future will decide in that ex parte way all disputed claims that may arise in this country. It is peculiarly dangerous for Parliament to make such a precedent when the claim is one that affects strongly,-and under' the circumstances very rightly,-the feeling of a very large and important body.

Mr. Speaker, this is an important claim, in regard to which it is important that justice should be done. Notwithstanding what the hon. gentleman has said, we have gone as far as it is possible for us to go to secure justice in the matter, namely, to secure a regular opportunity for these men to be heard. I have not one word to take back of what I said, and whatever may properly be taken from it will in proper time and place, I have no doubt, be implemented. But I have to say here tonight, perfectly frankly, that for my part I will have no share or part in any action which is in effect most absolutely subversive of the settled institutions of this country. I can imagine no greater evil that could come to the people of this country or of any country than that they should see the place and the functions of their courts of justice usurped by the Houses of Parliament, and that they should find themselves subject to having claims against them adjudicated upon by the Houses of Parliament, that these claims should be withdrawn from the jurisdiction of the courts and from the application by the courts of the laws of this country. There may be cases where it might be a right and a proper thing if it be found by judicial decision that in certain cases the laws as they stand do not operate to produce justice, for Parliament to come to the rescue with a remedy. But this is the first time in my experience that I have heard it suggested that it was the proper function of Parliament to decide of its own authority- to decide, so far as the great bulk of us fMr. Doherty.]

are concerned, without knowledge of the actual facts of this case-the claims of one party of men, no matter how important they may be, against another man or another body of men, even if it be a corporation. I have no desire to look for or impute any improper motives in this particular instance, but may I just point out in a general way what the lesson of such an action would be? It is this: That persons who are members of a large and important section of the people of this country, members of a body well organized, and properly so, in defence of their rights in the future will have nothing to do when they think they have been wronged but to come and put their case before this Parliament, and without provision for the hearing of those against wdiom their claims are made they will get from this Parliament, under guise of legislation, a judgment condemning the adverse party. The hon. gentleman has referred to unrest and to the effect failure to act in the manner he suggests might have on that unrest. For my part I cannot conceive of anything that would he more apt to create the most absolute lack of confidence in this Parliament and in our parliamentary institutions than that we should be guilty of such a usurpation oi power. We must face what would be said, and what would be pleaded-and the circumstances would give! colour to it, -namely, that we were doing this because of the great power and great influence of this large section of the people to whom the men here concerned belonged and whose sympathies are entirely with the men here concerned.

Surely we do not want to give circulation to that idea. Surely we do not want to create the belief that justice is to be administered in accordance with the political power that can be wielded by bodies of men who may be interested in particular cases.

I am satisfied that the well-thinking, sane workingmen of this country will realize what an infinitely valuable' privilege it is for them to have the security and protection of the courts. If we intervene to-day to deal with this claim upon their statement and out of deference to their feelings, what guarantee will they have that tomorrow, when they may have difficulties with some of the very great and powerful bodids with whom they more or less frequently come in contact-bodies which are reputed, at all events, to exercise some influence over Parliament-they will not find themselves exposed to the danger of Parliament undertaking, without hearing their views, to wipe
out their claim, because of a belief, honest if you will, on the part of certain members of Parliament, that the contentions of the adverse parties were sound, and just,, and well-founded?

No, Mr. Speaker. When we appeal in the name of justice, let us remember that real justice is in the keeping of the different bodies that are concerned with the control of the government of the country in their proper spheres. There rightly belongs to this Parliament a legislative function, as. there rightly belongs to the courts a judicial function; and to night we are asked not only to usurp the judicial function of the courts, but, after we have done so, to act in a manner in which no court in any British country would ever dream of acting: we are asked to sanction and lay down the principle that henceforth in this country disputed claims shall be determined and adjudicated without hearing the parties against whom they are made, and without giving them any opportunity to open their mouths.

And what is the appalling consequence which it is said is liable to ensue if we do not do this? The awful consequence is that if it be found that these men have a moral and not a legal claim perhaps the people of Canada may have to pay these pensions. As I understand from the hon. gentlemen's expose of the case, it is probably the Provident Fund that in any event will pay the pensions if they have to be paid. But even if that be not so, I say , and it is my last word-that I will resolutely refuse to consent to such an abuse of Parliament's power, perpetrated at a moment when the gravest possible suspicions would be justified by its being exercised. Are not the circumstances worthy of remark? For the last ten years there 'have been Parliaments in this country,, as there have always been. During that time there was a Grand Trunk Railway Company in full operation, swaying a great influence, and being in * position to exercise that influence in elections as well as in other directions; and the hon. gentleman asks this Parliament to do now what could have been done during those ten years. It is only at the last moment, when the shareholders of the company cease to be such, when this Government has come to be die only shareholder, when consequently there can be no question of political influence in connection with the company that would affect in any way persons in this House or in the country,.-it is only at- that moment

that the hon. gentleman wakes up with a burst of heroic declamation and declaration that justice must be done, and asks Parliament to hasten to pronounce in favour of the only element concerned which in future is going to exercise political influence, and to render judgment without being in a position to act judicially, not having heard both parties.

I ask you, Mr. Speaker, could Parliament be asked to put itself in a more false position? Gould Parliament be asked to do anything more calculated to destroy public confidence in itself and in parliamentary institutions? I ask hon. members this question in the name of those very principles of justice,, properly understood, to which the hon. gentleman appeals; in the name of the respect which we all owe to the House of which we are members; in the name oi the respect which we owe to the well-established institutions of this country,, institutions which we have inherited from the Mother Country, and under which it is impossible that any man should arrogate to himself the right to pronounce condemnation against those who have not been afforded an opportunity of presenting their side of a dispute.

M,r. JEAN J. DENIS (Joliette): I should like to ask the Minister a question. In con nection with this matter there are -three alternatives. The pensions have to be forfeited, or they will be paid by the Grand Trunk Company, or they will be paid by the country. I desire to know which of these alternatives the Minister is advocating.

566461,ca.proc.d.1920-04-22.3.11.53,1920-04-22,2f5657db-e63e-47b8-8ff0-51286ffbc3e6,ca.m.2160,Mr. F. F. PARDEE (West Lambton):,,QUESTIONS.,BILL TO CONFIRM AGREEMENT WITH THE COMPANY.,,Mr. Speaker, I fully realize the fact, as was pointed out by the hon. member for Cape Breton North and Victoria (Mr. McKenzie) and the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty) that there might be some difficulty in bringing this particular claim before the Board of Arbitration without something enabling the Government to do so. Although

the Minister of Justice said he did not propose, any more than was possible, to find fault with the speech delivered by the leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King), nevertheless for an hour and a half he endeavoured to urge all that he possibly could against the arguments contained in that speech. Might I say that in my opinion in the minister's speech the mountain has laboured and brought forth a mouse. The great argument which he has advanced time and again to-night-iterated and reiterated-is the awful - consequences that would ensue were we who represent the people to take into consideration the claim which a considerable portion of the community had against a road that'this Government is taking over. The minister seems to regret and bewail the fact that our courts should be deprived of the right to adjudicate between the parties. He asked, was ever such a thing heard of? He went on to argue that the case is unprecedented. I admit with him-and I think many hon. gentlemen on both sides will admit-that the case is unprecedented. Why is it unprecedented? The Government, for some reason best known to themselves-is in an extraordinary hurry decided to take over the Grand Trunk Railway. If I recollect aright at the time that decision was reached, the railway was not supposed to have very much equity in it. Nevertheless, though there was no particular equity there, the Government, out of the goodness of its heart, appointed a Board of Arbitration- for what reason I never could conceive- saying to that board: We have taken this road over but to those people you shall not pay more than a certain amount of money and vre will guarantee certain stock. It certainly was unprecedented, absolutely unprecedented, for the people of Canada to take over something and guarantee something that had not value. Is it not unprecedented also for the Minister of Justice to say to the men who have put forth their claim in a just, proper and fitting way before the people and have substantiated it: We have only heard the case ex parte. For the minister to say this is only a play upon words, a splitting of hairs. The House and the country has known the facts lor years and years, ever since the strike was undertaken and settled. The question has been openly discussed during all that time and both sides have been fully heard. Therefore this is no ex parte hearing. Every member of the House is conversant with both sides of the question, and the Government, more particularly, is conversant with

every claim that the men have presented. Truly, the matter is unprecedented for the very reasons that I have given to the House: the Government has stepped in, has taken over a property, and is paying to the shareholders of that property something to which-to my mind -they are not and never were entitled, and at the same time taking from the pockets of employees enough money to cover the payment. It is all very well for the Minister of Justice to stand here and advance the contention he did when the facts are as apparent as daylight. He refers to the leader of the Opposition as a protector of the men; and as one who was concerned in the making of the agreement that was entered into. Therefore, he contends it was. the fault of the Liberal Government that the pensions to the men were not taken care of. Sir, it is plain that upon the present Government rests the responsibility of seeing that these men are paid or otherwise. But in order to shirk their plain duty the Government is shifting the blame onto the Liberal Administration and saying; We are free; they made the bargain and we did not, and hence we will do nothing. That is absolutely their argument here tonight. In so many words that is the argument of the Minister of Justice; and I submit, 'Sir, that it is unworthy of the minister or the Government he represents.

What are the facts? There was a settlement made with the men. And in that connection the Minister of Justice asked: What was the leader of the Opposition doing, what was his business there? The object of the leader of the Opposition in taking part in those proceedings was to endeavour as between the men and the company, to settle a matter that was of great interest to the people of this country,

*a matter that affected every man, woman and child in the Dominion. He was, Sir, doing his whole duty as a member of the Government of that time to the people whom he represented. I would commend his example to my hon. friends opposite. I would suggest to them that they should do as much justice to the people as the leader of the Opposition did when the opportunity was open to him.

The men's claim appears to me so patent, so self evident and so absolutely legitimate that it is only a case of "" pig on pork "" to pile up the argument in support of their contention. The men went out on strike. Many of those who went out remained out but a very short time, and returned to duty, we know in some cases, at the re-

quest of the company. They did so because they were old and valued employees of the company, and the company was under the impression that their presence on the road might help to a large extent to settle the grievances as between themselves and the men. Those men are asking to-day that they be paid their pension but are debarred from receiving it. A tentative agreement was drawn up, and let me cite the first portion of it from a statement which is headed "" Memorandum of certain Railway Conductors against the Pension Fund of the Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada"" :

The company were thereby empowered to make payments to the pension fund out of the gross revenue as part of the working expenses in priority to all the ordinary and preferred creditors of the company. The claims upon this fund were thereafter a substantial term in the conditions of employment and were not a gratuity or bounty which the company were entitled to give or withhold at their whim or pleasure.

The labour of these men contributed to swell the gross earnings of the company, and was sunk in them for the benefit of others if this claim goes unrecognized. That is a short statement of the facts. It was not a gratuity, it was not a bounty, it was an absolutely executed contract as between the Grand Trunk Railway Company and the men, that in consideration of performing certain services-which the men did perform-a pension should be paid to them in their old age.

That was the understanding, Mr. Speaker, upon which these men entered the employ of the Grand Trunk Railway Company, that was the 'understanding they worked under for years. TJpon being taken back they *were promised that that understanding would never be broken, and they are to-day under the terms of that understanding still entitled to their pensions. Why do I say that? Because, 'Sir, the. Grand Trunk Railway Company agreed-and I am not concerned as to the length of time that elapsed, as to when the men were to be taken back or otherwise, the Grand Trunk Railway Company, I say, even if they did not set it out in black and white, tacitly agreed, there is not a shadow of a doubt, as I have already stated, viz:

Whereas the Government then in power effected settlement, and it was agreed, among other things, that the employees would return to work and resume their standing in the service and their seniority rights.
Their standing in the service."" What does the word ""standing"" or ""status""

mean, Sir? In my humble opinion, the whole case turns upon what is to be interpreted from the clause which practically re-engages those men? The interpretation, as I have taken it from the Imperial dictionary-which, I am told, is by Order in Council the dictionary adopted by the Government in order to get the meaning of words and the substance thereof-is in these words:
Status n. (L) 1. Standing or position as regards rank or condition. ""A phrase

decisive of a man's social status"". O. W. Holmes.-2. Position of affairs-status quo, the condition in which the thing or things were at first; as, a treaty between belligerents, which leaves each party in status quo ante helium, that is, with the same possession and rights they had before the war began.

The same status, the same right, and in the same position that they occupied before the war began. The position they occupied ""before the war began"" was that they were employed in certain capacities, they received certain wages under contract, they, moreover, under that contract, knew that certain sums were paid into the Provident or Insurance Fund that would enure to their benefit upon their ceasing their employment in a legitimate way. They ceased their employment, I will admit, only to a degree. But, for the sake of argument, even although they did cease their employment they went back to service at the request of the oompany to resume their old status; in other words, to be put back in every particular where they were before.

I submit to this House, and I am not afraid, notwithstanding the fact that the Minister of Justice seems to be so absolutely appalled at the results that may flow therefrom-I am not in the least afraid, Sir, if simple justice is done to those men, as is prayed by them, that the people of this country will have anything but commendation for the Government that does it. When you take a large body of such intelligent men, some of them even intellectual men, men of the very highest class of skilled labour, and say to them: We as a government are taking over that road, although we know you have certain claims outstanding, and although we and the people of this country know that a large amount of money is being paid to shareholders that should not be paid, and part of it is your money-all I have to say to any government that takes such a course is: They had better beware.

,Unionist (Liberal),,Frederick Forsyth Pardee,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=2f5657db-e63e-47b8-8ff0-51286ffbc3e6&Language=E&Section=ALL

Oh, he says, I am so anxious about these men. He indeed begged, in the presence of the Speaker of the House, that no other member of Parliament of that day would ever have to encounter the perils he encountered or go through what he went through in standing between these two great warring factions and trying to bring them together. In the whole course of the fifteen months of the agreement and up to the time the Laurier

Government went out of power, the hon. member never brought to the attention of this House that the Grand Trunk had broken their agreement in declining to reestablish the pension rights of the men. But, he says, the Grand Trunk came to the Government and wanted millions of money, but we would not give it to them because they had not carried out the agreement that they bound themselves to carry out. At that time certainly they had not carried it out; they had not put the men back at all. That waited for the next government to accomplish. Well, they had not carried it out, and so he says: When the Grand Trunk came to us for millions of money we turned a deaf ear to them and said, ""we cannot listen to you at all because you have not carried out your agreement."" Would it not be interesting to know what these millions were for that the Government in 1911 was going to give the Grand Trunk only for the fact that they had not carried out their strike agreement of the year before? What millions were in contemplation to be advanced to the Grand Trunk at that time? It was never made known to the country that millions were waiting to be given to the Grand Trunk if they only carried out their agreement with their employees entered into with the hon. member. In one vray it may be a good thing perhaps that this difficulty arise and that the hon. member became the obstacle to legislation that certainly could not have been of very much advantage to us. It is a pity that something of that kind had not arisen about seven years before for it might have saved this country a whole lot of trouble now. But what does the hon. member mean by saying?-We refused to pass money Bills giving the Grand Trunk money, because they did not carry out their agreement, but we passed other Bills granting other things to the Grand Trunk, allowing them to buy other roads and invest in their bonds, and guarantee $30,000,000 of stock for the Great North Western Railway. If it was worth while for him to stand in the way of an important Bill, surely it was more important that he should stand in the

way of a less important Bill. But all the Bills were of importance and no doubt essential to the Grand Trunk that the hon. member let several pass and never said a word. The others that he says he dropped we never heard of until now.

566505,ca.proc.d.1920-04-22.3.11.97,1920-04-22,d02a7b53-dad0-4944-82b0-aed9054a7bc2,ca.m.4870,Mr. METGHEN:,Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs,QUESTIONS.,BILL TO CONFIRM AGREEMENT WITH THE COMPANY.,,I do not think, Mr. Speaker, that the hon. member at least should complain of your ruling. Now in the next place-aside entirely from the incongruity of the whole thing, the helplessness of the position the hon. member in trying to claim one thing in one breath and another in another-*what would be the position of this Parliament if such an . amendment were to pass? What could the Grand Trunk say to us, what could the citizens of countries everywhere say to this Parliament if we accepted this amendment? They would say to us first of all: The claim of the men, if it exists, is against the Provident and Pension Fund of the Grand Trunk. Now I do not know just -what responsibility the Grand Trunk has for that Provident and Pension Fund, but it would occur to me as pretty obvious that there were others who were interested in that besides the Grand Trunk. It would appear to me that the other beneficiaries were largely interested in the Provident and Pension Fund. Is Parliament possessed of information as to the various constituent claims and their relative rights in the Provident and Pension Fund, sufficient to justify Parliament in arrogating to itself the functions of a court of justice, and simply on the motion of the leader of the Opposition dispensing with all those rights, wiping out everything that may exist, and fastening on this Provident and Pension Fund a claim that possibly others interested in it may dispute altogether aside altogether from the claims of the Grand Trunk Railway Company? Certainly Parliament is in possession of no such information, and I venture to assert there is not one hon. member of this House, not even the leader of the Opposition, who, it he were constituted a judge in this matter, is to-day in possession of evidence to say

what other claimants there may be ai against that Provident Fund who have a right to consideration, and whose claims should not lightly be wiped away without their being here, apart altogether from the Grand Trunk itself. Certainly the Grand Trunk could say to us, and every citizen of every country could say to us for all time: It does not matter what property rights we have, you dispose of them without letting us make a claim to them and without hearing us; after you have created courts of justice to dispose of such claims, you take from those courts the functions you vested in them, and arrogate them to yourself: is that a good country to invest money in, is that a country to which we should give the credit of our financee? It would appear to me that the answer would be obvious.

Then in the next place the Grand Trunk and everybody else could say to us: Why did you not do this before? If you wanted to make a claim against us, if you wanted to stand behind these men and make yourselves identical with them in interest and force their claim against us why did you wait nine years before you did it? You say that there are certain implications that the circumstances of the time gave a moral claim to certain parties to that agreement. Why did you wait till almost 'all had gone to their graves? Sir Frederick Borden was one of the parties to the agreement; he is now dead. Mr. Hays was there, and the hon. member berates the memory of Mr. Hays, long since in his grave. Mr. Wain-wright was a prominent party to the negotiations; he also is dead. Sir Wilfrid Laurier w>as the party to whom the hon. member directed his interminable letter; he is dead. And we are not even favoured with Sir Wilffrid Laurier's reply to that epistle. The parties to that controversy have passed away, and after all that has taken place, the hon. member says that now is the time to enforce eternal justice and for us who survived to say that we know all the circumstances, that we know the claim of the men is all right, and that nothing can be said against it, and we are going to decide it now once for all. For fifteen months the hon. member sat in this House as a member of the Government and never asserted this right. His party sat in opposition for eight years more and never suggested that there was such a right. Last year, when this Parliament was fixing the terms of the agreement, authorizing its provisions one by one that were to be made between the Grand Trunk and the Government of

Canada, the hon. member sat silent and never (thought there was any claim he should urge at ,all. What would he answer to the Grand Trunk when the Grand Trunk says to him: Why didn't you, before this matter came to us for consideration, have at least the courtesy to get up and say in Parliament that some such clause as this should be embodied in the agreement so that we could put it before our shareholders for consideration? What would be the answer of the hon. member? No answer at all. The political merit of the thing from his point of view had not dawned on him at that time, and did not until this session.-that is the only answer he could give that would ever be believed by any one. Now he comes and says: It is true that a year ago when I was at full liberty to move that a clause be inserted in the agreement fastening a civil liability upon the Grand Trunk I failed to move it, I failed to see that such a clause was laid before the other parties to the contract, I failed utterly even to .mention the subject in Parliament. The agreement was made pursuant to the authority of this Hopse, and this House bound itself in honour to accept it if accepted by the Grand Trunk Company. That agreement authorized by Parliament, was submitted . by this House and by the country to the Grand Trunk as embodying our view of what was fair and right to be included, and we said to the Grand Trunk: These are our terms; if you agree to them we are bound. The Grand Trunk did agree to them. Now, after all that has taken place, the hon. member comes and says that now is the time to change the whole thing and to inject into the agreement, after the event, a clause he never thought of during all these nine or, ten years.

One would have thought that the debate that took place in the House on Friday night last would have satisfied the hon. gentleman forever of the absurdity of the position he has taken in this matter. I do not recall in the history of Parliament a more absurd and incongruous suggestion that that there should be attached to the agreement-it does not matter whether or not it is a part of the agreement in forma, for it becomes if passed in effect and substance a most vital part of it-the confession that after both parties have agreed upon the matter, and after our having said a year ago that we had made up our mind as to what we would do, we have found it necessary to wheel about now and tell the Grand Trunk that we did not know our own minds before but have

awakened now .to the sense of a great injustice and are going to change the agreement entirely and reverse the position we took at our last session. Surely that reflection is sufficient to bring home to the hon. gentleman's mind the very distressing conviction that it is unfair to the intelligence of Parliament that it should be asked to take that humiliating position not only before the people of our own country but before the people of Great Britain as well, who are watching our proceedings at the present time.

Even if there were some merit in the hon. gentleman's suggestion and some consistency in his conduct, surely-having said to the Grand Trunk: "" These are our terms, do you agree to them or not? and having received their reply: Yes, we agree to them,""-we are in honour bound to abide by these terms and not present the equivocating, vacillating, twisting position of thinking of something else a year after the event, and suggesting additions after both parties had concurred as to what the exact arrangement should be.

Now to resume my quotations: January 2, 62; January 12, 621; January 20, 621; February 2, 65; February 10, 66; February 24, 66; March 2, 65; March 16, 641; March 26, 63; April 12, 601; April 15, 601. Then on the 19th of April financial writers were urging the holders of Grand Trunk Rail-

way stocks not to throw them away at the present prices. The common stock was then worth 5J and the guaranteed fours, 55, or 71 points below what they were on September 3. Surely it is clear that the hon. gentleman was wholly wrong in arguing his appreciation. Certainly this reduction is in no way due to the legislation. Indeed it was very likely, as we all admitted at the time, that there would be a small, but still appreciable, increase. That was due to the legislation and it could not be avoided. However it was very small indeed, and not sufficient to counteract the depreciation that was due to' the increased value of money; and as a result of the two forces working together those shareholders are today worth millions less than they were when the negotiations were on, and prior to the conclusion of those negotiations. Consequently the impression that hon. gentlemen opposite assiduously sent abroad that we had by this legislation, quoting the words of the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's, handed out fifteen millions, maybe twenty millions, maybe thirty millions, filched from the pockets, he said, of the people of Canada for these shareholders by this legislation-that impression so scattered abroad by hon. members is wholly false. It is wholly unjust to the people of this country, wholly unjust to the Government of Canada, and wholly unworthy of the hon. gentlemen themselves.

The hon. gentleman predicted that instead of the figures I have given there would be this result: Why, he said, these four per cent guaranteed stocks are now at 70, and they will go to 80 right away, and they will be at 100 shortly. That is how he made up his figures. It shows how cautious hon. members should be especially when they attempt to speak as to the future in regard to matters of this kind. It shows furthermore that that feature of the arrangement -which was most severely criticized by hon. gentlemen opposite at a time when they never dreamed of the subject matter of to-night's debate-that feature of the arrangement so far from being unjust to the Canadian people and a great boom and advantage to the Grand Trunk shareholders, was fair and equitable as between them both and meant no advantage at a"" to those shareholders beyond what they were entitled to, and meant no loss nor anything but simple justice' to the people of Canada whom we represent.

566524,ca.proc.d.1920-04-22.3.11.116,1920-04-22,2555053a-03ba-40ed-a2fb-de4f35b5fca4,ca.m.4960,Mr. ALPHONSE VERVILLE (St. Denis):,,QUESTIONS.,BILL TO CONFIRM AGREEMENT WITH THE COMPANY.,,I do not want to let the occasion pass withflir. Meighen.]

out going on record in favour of the amendment. For the good reason that I am not a lawyer 1 am not going to follow the argument of my hon. friend who has just taken his seat. It seemed to me that part of the time he was asking questions of hon. gentlemen on this side probably in the hope of eliciting something upon which to make a point.

I do wish however to consider some of the arguments the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty) has indulged in. To my mind his reasoning with respect to the amendment was ineffective: If the men are entitled to the pension-such is the wording of the amendement-they will get it; if they are not entitled to the pension they will not receive it. Where is the harm then in the House making a pronouncement on the subject? This Parliament is the council of the nation, the highest tribunal of the country, and therefore the proper place, from which such a pronouncement should issue. The Minister of Justice tells us that if the men have any rights they can go to the courts. My hon. friend apparently has not yet forgotten that he was' on the judicial bench for fifteen years,, and therefore whenever anything of this kind comes up he is always in favour of a reference to the legal tribunals. He admitted that if there was not a legal obligation there might be a moral obligation with respect to the men's claim. I would remind the House that the Minister of Justice knows what it means to draw a pension. In his case, is there a legal, or a moral obligation involved? To my mind it is questionable whether there is. any moral obligation on his part to draw a pension in view of the position which he occupies in the Government at the present time.

The Minister has also told us that there was plenty of opportunity when the leader df the Opposition occupied the office of Minister of Labour for the men to advance their claim. I have not yet heard that during that time there was any opportunity afforded for putting in a claim, for the very good reason that none of the men had put in that period of service entitling them to a pension. The ex-Minister of Labour has told us tonight-at least I understood it that way-that had this question been put before him when the reinstatement of the men was being argued he would have seen to its adjustment. But the position of affairs was that, there being a pension fund and the men being reinstated after the strike-a strike is legitimate, it is re-
cognized by the law, it is not an illegal affair-they resumed their former status and were entitled to receive their pension.

The argument has been made that at that time the men did not care about the matter of pension. But I know exactly how these questions operate. Workingmen will not bind themselves so that they will be at the mercy of big corporations, or in fact any employer, for the sake of a pension. It seems to me that they are perfectly en-titjed to be restored to their old positions. If since 1910 the then Liberal Government, according to the ex-Minister of Labour (Mr. Mackenzie King), refused to give any help to the Grand Trunk Railway Company on account of that company not doing the right thing by their employees, I think his Government were quite justified in their refusal, and he took the right course in endorsing that refusal. Now that occasion presents itself to help these men have their just claims recognized, I do not see why the Government should decline to put in concrete form what would secure payment of these pensions to those who are really entitled to them.'

As an excuse for not taking such action we are told that the matter will go .before a board of arbitration. Well, in the past, Mr. Speaker, anything pertaining to labour that has gone before any board of arbitration representing organized capital has been treated in such a way that I do not blame these employees, or any other employees, for their lack of confidence in such boards.

As I stated at the outset, Mr. Speaker, I want to put on record my belief that it is absolutely unfair for the Government not to accept the proposed amendment. I am not speaking from the legal standpoint, because if I were a lawyer I would be trying to split hairs after the fashion of my hon. friend (Mr. Meighen) who has just taken his seat. If the Government does not accept this amendment, the public at large and the working people in particular will infer that the Government is afraid to guarantee to these men their claims in connection with the pension fund, and that it prefers to protect the big interests against the just claims of these men. I would not like that impression to go abroad, and 1 therefore point out to the Government that their only way of salvation is to accept this amendment.
It must be borne in mind that whenever men are returned to their positions after a strike under the terms stated here tonight, it is well understood that such re-100i

turn means everything connected with their positions. This is not a technical question of law, it is purely a question of the wording of the agreement, and I can see no grounds for any other interpretation than that which the men placed on the wording of the agreement under which they agreed to terminate the strike. Therefore I want to go on record as being in favour of this amendment, which, I repeat, is but a fair and just recognition of the claims of the men-; and I also want to warn the Government that unless they wish the impression to go broadcast throughout the Dominion that they are going to favour big corporations rather than do evenhanded justice to the workingmen of this country, the best course for them to follow is to accept this-amendment.

MORPHY (North Perth):,,QUESTIONS.,BILL TO CONFIRM AGREEMENT WITH THE COMPANY.,,My views have been already given, Mr. Speaker, on this question, and I am very strongly in favour of the men receiving equitable treatment in some way. But I do complain a little about the hon. leader of the Opposition attempting, as I would say,, to shirk responsibility. He was the man in charge of the negotiations between the company and the men at the time this trouble arose, he put himself in the midst of the difficulties, and he has confessed to-night that he ~was present at the drafting of the agreement,-which is pretty close contact with the situation. If he was present at that drafting he was a part and parcel of that agreement so far as his intermediary work was concerned, and he certainly cannot escape responsibility for what he failed to bring about.

What did he fail to bring about? The two things over which this discussion has arisen: First,, the pensions of the men which he says were spoken of at the time and dealt with as a separate matter. I ask him why those pensions were dealt with as a separate matter. It was one of the main rights among the many rights that tlie men claimed. It is all very well for him to say that the matter was spoken of by the men as of no account, but to-day he speaks of it as being considered by the men to be of great account. Where is his statement that the men have made it of such great account? Were they the same men who told him in 1910 that the matter of pensions was of no account? We have the hon. gentleman's statement, and we are bound to take it, but it is absolutely unsubstantiated by any outside evidence of pressure being brought to bear upon him, either by the men who then -said pensions were of no account or by the men whom he pretends, voluntarily I believe,, to represent to-day. The matter of pensions, therefore, is left out of the agreement which the hon. gentleman sat by and saw drafted. That

is one thing that was left out, through his supineness and neglect, I would -say: left out through the carelessness with which he approached the serious matter in. hand, or on account of some other influence than that of the men.

, Then, what is the next thing that is left out? The date within which the men should be reinstated. The most humiliating thing I have heard for many day is the confession of the leader of the Opposition who comes into this House and says: I was at the drafting of that agreement; I was pa!rt and parcel of it: my whole soul was stirred with a desire to bring about an agreement that would be full and fair and complete; but I left out a most important thing-the date at which the men should be reinstated, I allowed the railway auhorities to put in that Bill abstract words to the effect that the men should be reinstated or put back as soon as possible. ""As soon as possible"", what a shilly-shally, lacking-in-executive, abstract way to draw an agreement! What a confession for an hon. gentleman to make who was present at the drafting of the agreement and who did not intervene in an attempt to make its provisions more specific ! Then, on the side, my hon. friend says: But I got from Mr. Wainwright and other gentlemen, not their agreement, not their undertaking under seal, but their word that I would be entitled to telegraph to the men that the phrase <as soon as possible meant that they would be taken back within ninety days. This also is left out, and at the eleventh hour my hon. friend, feeling that his efforts on that occasion resulted in such a mess, and perhaps with a view of trying to reinstate himself with the men and bring himself back into their good graces, springs up here with a claptrap resolution seeking to curry favour with the men whose interests he absolutely ignored, and failed properly to represent.
Now, what is the resolution that he asks us to support? He asks that a clause be added to the Bill to this effect:

Any right or any interest of any employee of the Grand Trunk Railway Company existing in the pension system prior to the strike of the company's employees which occurred in July, 1910, is hereby declared not to have been affected by the said strike or any circumstance or condition arising out of or in connection therewith.
Now, what does that mean? The hon. gentleman argues that the whole thing is affected by an agreement which impliedly was to reinstate the men in their former positions with all their pensions and all

the other conditions of their employment. Yet I am asked to support a resolution which declares exactly the opposite, because the agreement was a condition or circumstance arising out of the strike. We have to take the agreement as it is. In it pensions are not provided for. I myself think that they are impliedly provided for. Then I accept the view of the Minister of Justice that when this board of arbitration gets seated and becomes seized of the issue of valuation, he'will make every effort to see that this claim is properly brought before that forum. I assume that the men will have every opportunity of presenting their claims. If the claim is found to be a legal one, then the men will get justice by that tribunal. The country is pledged to justice; this House is pledged to justice, either from a legal or from an equitable point of view. If the arbitrators find that there is no legal claim, the Minister of Justice says that the matter will be taken up by Parliament. I have already had occasion to say, and I say it again, that this Parliament is the highest forum of equity in this Dominion, and if the board of arbitrators find that they cannot deal with this matter, Parliament, with all the parties before it and after proper consideration, will have to deal with it. But the company have no right to ask to be relieved because the Government is taking over all the assets and properties of the system. I am not frightened by the cry which the leader of the Opposition raises to-night that it is the shareholders of the Grand Trunk Railway Company who should pay. Probably it is, but if we are not able to compel them to pay and the arbitration cannot work the matter out, surely this House is big enough, and the country is big enough, to recognize the equitable right which these men undoubtedly have. I do not believe in splitting hairs. I did not follow with much approval the argument about the words ""put back"" or ""reinstated,""-they mean the same thing to me. The clear intention of the agreement, so poorly drawn, was that the strike was to be an end of all trouble and that the men were to go back to their former positions and status in the employ of the company. In other words, the full intention of the agreement was that the men were to be reinstated and to be given possession of all the rights which they had previously enjoyed. ""Under these circumstances, and on account of the peculiar wording of the agreement, I prefer to support the attitude taken by the Government. The Minister of the Interior (Hon. Mr. Meiglien)

claims that there is a legal right. The Minister of Justices promises to support the attitude which I wish to see adopted in connection with the claim put forward- an attitude favourable to the men before the board of arbitration. I prefer to trust, the Government and its perfectly clear-cut declarations, rather than the eleventh-hour attempt of the leader of the Opposition by pretend to be the friend of men whose interests he so flagrantly failed to safeguard at a time when he was responsible for the proper wording of a contract which should have been clear and specific,-a contract so carelessly drawn as to create the doubts which have brought on this discussion today.

,Unionist,,Hugh Boulton Morphy,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=99359485-a884-4818-b289-348ffbe33fb1&Language=E&Section=ALL

FIELDING:,,QUESTIONS.,BILL TO CONFIRM AGREEMENT WITH THE COMPANY.,,Mr. Speaker, I do not rise for the purpose of participating in the general discussion, I had no intention of speaking oil the motion; I simply want to make a brief comment with regard to the little controversy that the Minister of the Interior (Hon. Mr. Meighen) and I had a few minutes ago concerning the quotations for certain stock, known as four per rent guaranteed stock, prior to the matte1' engaging the attention of the Government, and the later quotations. The period that has since passed has been a period of severe financial depression when all financial conditions have been Unfavourable. There is the further thought that we must have in mind, namely, that this transaction is not yet complete. The Government guarantee does not rest on that 4 per cent guaranteed stock; it is only in expectation that the market has been affected; the full fruition of the advance has yet to come.

The point of difference between the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Meighen) and myself, is this, that the stock has gone to 65 and 66 and so forth, and he has intimated in effect that that is a mere trifle, a few points beyond the quotations of the earlier times. He has made his comparisons between the 65 and 66 of recent days and quotations of an earlier date, which, without being specific, he gave us to understand were only a trifle less. With his permission, I interrupted him to say that my recollection, on which I based the argument, was that the four per cent stock had been 45, and that the contrast should be made between the 45 and whatever increased value the stock had. I have since then had an opportunity to turn up Hansard, and I find on page 1074, October 16, 1919, speaking of this guaranteed stock, I said:
Now that stock has some value. It was ' quoted in the London market not very long : ago-I am so informed; I have not been able to prove that statement by reference, but I believe it is correct-at 45.

I remember the circumstance, that a brother member assured me that he had seen the quotation at 45; but as I did not have the quotation before me, I was careful to say that I gave the figure at 45 because I was so informed; I believed it to be correct. and I am satisfied now it was correct. I made this quotation from one of the London financial papers:
There has been a sharp burst in Grand Trunk issues on the notification that the matter in dispute is likely to be submitted to arbitration-

That was' long before we toad the document submitted to us here. They had knowledge or impression of it in England although we were not permitted to know if it here*. When I said that from memory I madeythat quotation at 45 and based my argument on that, the minister saiid that he was not concerned at what it might have been years before. This was, however, only a few weeks or days before. Moreover, I find that the minister himself, in, reply to my argument, made a quotation just a little above 45, and yet he said that I would have to go back years for a quotation of that kind. I quote from the minister him-settf as reported on page 1024 of Hansard :
Mr. Meighen: (Resuming): I was referring to certain quotations in the London Times. I find that on September 18, Grand Trunk common stock was quote at 9 7/8, 9 15/16, and so on,-
We are not dealing with the common stock.
-that the 4 per cent guaranteed stock was quoted at 49}, 49g, *50}.
That was after the agreement bad taken place*, so* that white the minister said that I would have to go back years for that quotation, he is answered by his own words .as shown' in* the debate.

Mr- D. D. McKENZIE (Gape Breton North 'and Victoria) : I listened with a great deal of interest .and attention to the legal gladiators who were dealing with this question to-night, and I imagine that the pensioners who are looking for their money, and their wives and children*, are not concerned so much about the hair-splitting and clever repartee that we may get from the leading lawyers of the Government as they are in, getting their money. I do not think it is an answer to the labouring classes of this country, whose interests are at stake and who look to this Parliament for their
LMr. Fielding.]
rights and protection, for the Government to say:
column2: Oh, some years back, ten* years

column1: ago, somebody did not make the agreement as clear as it might possibly be, and consequently yon have no rights. I wish particularly to bring to the notice of the House to-night a resolution of the men involved and particularly concerned in this matter, a resolution which was submitted to the Government in May of last* year. The stock in tirade of the Government to-night, of the Minister of Justice (Mr.' Doherty) and of the Minister of the Interior, (Mr. Meighen) is that we on this side of the House slept on our rights if we were representing those men, and their claims were not placed sufficiently before Parliament, That cannot bold water for one moment in view of a resolution passed in May, 1919, at a meeting ait which some hundred delegates were present. These are the facta which the railwaymen submitted to the Government in May, 1919, when the Grand Trunk acquisition Act was not drafted, when there was not a word about it:

Whereas we believe Parliament, though it did not so provide in the Act, surely intended that the said Pension Fund would be administered by the Pension Department of the Railways fairly and without discrimination ; and, Whereas the said company, through its Pension Department has debarred its employees form the benefits of the said Pension Fund because they participated in a strike of the Conductors, Brakemen, and Yardmen, on the road in 1910, and,

Whereas, it is well known that the said strike was the result of the unreasonable attitude assumed by -its then management, in refusing to grant the employees increased wages and improved working conditions based on the standard wage and conditions on other Canadian railways, and.
Whereas, it is well known that the transportation brotherhoods, including .the Order of Railway Conductors, do not strike until all other means of settlement have been exhausted, and,
Whereas, the employees who participated in the strike of 1910 had the sympathy of the citizens generally and especially those citizens located along the said railway, and,

Whereas, tfie Government then in power effected a settlement, and it was agreed among other things that the employees would return to work and resume their standing in the service and their seniority rights held by them prior to the strike, as though they had been continuously in the service, and,

Whereas, the company has since the said agreement deprived the said employees who have retired from the service on account of the age limit from the benefits of the Pension Fund, alleging that their participation in the strike in 1910, broke their continuity of service with the company, and,

Whereas, many conductors and other train men that had served the company and the public faithfully and continuously up to fifty-three (53) years, and having reached the age limit have been retired from the service, and for the
reason above stated debarred from the pension which they so sorely need on account of the low wages in effect on this road prior to the strike of 1910, and,

Whereas, the accredited representatives or the Order of Railway Conductors and Brotherhood of Railway Trainmen having appealed to the management of the Grand Trunk Railway, and also to its Board of Directors domiciled in England, and its Chairman, Mr. Smithers, for the restoration of the said pensions without success, and in pursuance of the policy ot these organizations to exhaust all legitimate efforts to reach a peaceful adjustment of all matters affecting the interests of their membership, therefore be it

Resolved: that we respectfully petition the Government and Parliament of Canada- to use their good offices to the end that the Grand Trunk Railway Company s Pension Department shall recede from its unjust attitude, and that in future it shall administer the Pension Fund of that company fairly and without, discrimination, and that it shall pay to its em-Dloyees all arrears of pension due them, ana,

Whereas, we are advised that our Government is desirous of acquiring the Grand Trunk railway and incorporating it as part of our National Railway system, and is negotiating to that end, therefore, be it further,

Resolved, that we respectfully petition our Government not to conclude said negotiations for the purchase of Ahe said Grand Trunk railway without providing for the protection of the pension interests of the employees concerned,
and be it further,
Resolved, that we furnish a copy of these resolutions to the Prime Minister, Sir Robert Borden, and to the following ministers of departments, and members of Parliament, name
ly;__The Honourable Minister of Railways, .T.
D Reid [DOT] the Hon. Minister of Labour, G. D. Robertson, and J. E. Armstrong, Esq., M.P., Chairman of the Railway Committee of the House of Commons.

That is the resolution that was submitted to the Prime Minister ('Sir Robert Borden) and to several other ministers in June ot last year, and, I presume, to the hon. member for West Lambton, (Mr. Pardee) representing that part of the country in which these men live. Is there any excuse for the Government not dealing with this question when the facts were so forcefully and clearly set forth before they started to negotiate for the taking over of this road? I think it is mere trifling to say that because ten years ago something happened which perhaps might have been avoided by a more conclusive agreement, we should not now' deal with this matter. We are now dealing with this corporation for the last time. It is being -wound up, as it were, it will soon go out of existence and vanish into thin air. When that opportunity is now before us, are we simply going to say that we will have nothing to do with the matter, and will give no remedy to these men, but will fall back on something which might have been done some years ago by people who had no power to do these things

by reason of the fact that the Government of which the Minister of Labour of that day was a member went out of power. We are told that this, that, and the other thing will be done. This question was before Parliament a few days ago, on the 12th of April, I believe, when the hon. member for North Simcoe (Mr. Currie) introduced his resolution. Everybody agreed upon the facts. No one questioned the facts as set forth by the hon. member for Simcoe and by the hon. memJber for West Lambton. I had sense enough to see that there wbuld be legal difficulties in the way. This claim arose in 1910, and the statute of_ limitations applies. The very moment this claim was raised before the board of arbitrators that is to he appointed, some lawyer representing ithe Grand Trunk would ask: When did this happen? The lawyer representing the claim of the men would have to admit that it happened in 1910. Then the Grand Trunk lawyer would point out to the legal tribunal that in the province of Ontario., where the claim arose, there was a statute of limitations, and that as the claim arose ten years ago no remedy could be given by the board, that the matter was out of their jurisdiction. Suppose the tribunal says: No, this is a moral claim, and we will disregard the statute of limitations and give judgment in favour of the men. There is a provision in this agreement for an appeal, not only to the Supreme Court of Canada, but to the Privy Council where the Grand Trunk would be at home with its friends; and I would ask any hon. member of this House how much show this finding of the hoard would have which was contrary to the statute of limitations, when it came before the Privy Council, and it was pointed out that moneys were taken from Englishmen which they were entitled to, and taken because, fors'ooth, there was a moral claim which was entirely barred by the statute of limitations in the province in which 'the claim arose. I submitted that the other day, and I was pushed aside by the hon. member for Simcoe as making an argument out of whole cloth. I did not get much sympathy from the Minister of Justice. He thought that the board could deal with this matter. I suggested, and it appears in Hansard, that the whole question should be submitted to a small committee of this House, where the Grand Trunk representatives and the representatives of the men would have an opportunity of appearing and telling their story, arid upon the committee's report such _ legislation could be passed as would be justified by

the facts submitted. That suggestion was also pushed aside by the Minister of Justice and the hon. member for Simcoe, as something that was not at all necessary. Now we are down to the point where there is no remedy at all. The Arbitration Board can do nothing at all because they have no jurisdiction, the claim is out of date. But in equity and fairness and honesty it still exists. Those who are familiar with the doctrine of the statute of limitations know that it is not the debt that is wiped out, but the remedy; the statute does not kill the debt, it debars the right of action. What I said the other day, and still say, is that Parliament should step in and wipe away these technicalities of the statute of limitations and other bars to the rights of these men, and legislate in such a way that their rights will be restored regardless of any statute of limitations. If the facts are admitted, what stands in the way of doing justice to these men? If the facts are not admitted let this whole business stand. There is no great rush to get it through today, and a committee of this House could be appointed to ascertain the facts and report to this House, upon which report legislation could be based doing justice to all concerned. If the men are not entitled to this money there is not a member here who is anxious to give it to them; if they are entitled to it, they should have it, and no autocratic conduct of any concern such as the Gran,d Trunk should be allowed to deprive them of their legitimate rights.

, The Act creating this fund was passed by this House in 1907. If it was conducted properly there must be a large accumulation of money in this fund. I am quite familiar with funds of this kind, because in our part of the country our workingmen in the mines and steel works contribute to funds of this kind, and in time large sums of money accumulate. If there is any change from one form of constitution to another, or from one form of association to another, the moneys so accumulated are passed over to the association that is to continue. I think my question of the Minister of Justice to-night, whether the fund which has been accumulating since 1907 was intact and would be passed over to the Government, was a very proper one. If it is intact, the Government has a perfect right to take the responsibilities and the liabilities in connection with that fund, but if there is no fund at, all, if the money has been utilized as it was coming in by the Grand Trunk, what right have we to pay their liabilities? ^We should take care that before

the Grand Trunk railway passes out of their hands, and we receive the property as being clear from debt and all liabilities, everything is settled and the mortgage wiped out. It is just as if a man were buying a house with a mortgage on it and was told:
column2: Oh, well, the man from whom you

column1: bought this house should have paid off this mortgage; he should have given you a clear title. The Government says: Never mind the mortgage, we will take over the property with the mortgage; we have lots of money and we can pay off the mortgage, and we will pay just the same amount for the property as if there was no mortgage on it. That is the attitude of the Government. But they must remember they are dealing with the money of the people, and there is no justification for paying any liabilities which the Grand Trunk should pay themselves. This is the last opportunity which we shall have to deal with this matter, and I submit that the rights of labour-and I have no business to call them labour because it is the rights of men who were members of an association , that we are discussing. It might be hinted that I am playing to Labour, but I am doing nothing of the kind. These men belonged to a society, call it what you will, and they are entitled to certain moneys which have been very improperly kept from them. This is the only tribunal in the world that has any jurisdictionto give the necessary remedy. Do not let us quibble over words; do not let us say:
column2: You

column1: should have done this; or: you should have done that, some years ago. The railway men in these societies care nothing about these quibbles; they are entitled to certain amounts of money, and this House can see that they get what they are entitled to, because we are taking over the property, and nothing should stand in the way of doing justice all round as between the company and the men. I hope sincerely that, before this property passes, these moneys that are due will be paid to the last cent.

Mr. F. N. MeCREA (Sherbrooke): Perhaps it might be a presumption on my part to criticise the statements of the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Meighen), since I am not a lawyer. But I do not quite agree with his views ! He read extensively from Hansard of 1910 in an endeavour to show that the attitude of the leader, of the Opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) at that time was quite at variance with his Ipresent stand. I fail to see that there is any inconsistency in the course which the leader of the Opposit-

ion has followed. The trouble occurred between the Grand Trunk and its employees, and the leader of the Opposition, then Minister of Labour, was entrusted with the task of effecting a settlement, which was finally brought about after considerable discussion and negotiation and after many interviews. The men agreed to return to work, and the company undertook to reinstate them, not as new men but as old employees. They were to resume the positions they held prior to the strike. Hansard of that time indicates that nothing was said at that time about pensions, but the fact, remains that the men agreed to return to work and the company agreed to take them back on their old standing. I-may be wrong, but I am firmly of the opinion that when the Company reinstated the men as old employees the men resumed the exact position in which they were before the strike in regard to pensions and everything else; and when no specific stipulation was made that they were being taken back on any new basis it cannot be contended now that they were not, and are not now, entitled to. pensions as if nothing had occurred. Some of the employees were taken back and some were not, but they have never ceased to complain that the Grand Trunk Compkny did not live up to their part of the agreement. The attitude of the leader of the Opposition today is that the company failed to live up to their agreement, and no quibbling will satisfy the men. Lawyers may be able to interpret things to suit themselves, but I see no difference between the attitude of the leader of the Opposition today and his attitude in 1910, and I see no reason whatever why the employees, taken back on the understanding that they were resuming their old status, are not fully justified in claiming whatever privileges that status carried with it.

The Minister endeavoured, to show that the Government had made a good bargain in taking over the Grand Trunk, and he argues that the date at which the stock should be valued is the date preceding the passage of the Bill through the House to acquire the railway. I think that if there was any stock on the market at that time it was difficult to ascertain what value it did have, until some element of the Government and their friends thought they would take over the Grand Trunk. Some emissaries of the Government went over from this country wirepulling or negotiating, and the stockholders of the Grand Trunk were led to believe that the road was going to be taken over on favourable conditions. That

might have been two, or three, or four months before the Bill was brought into the House, but whenever the sockholders got an inkling that the Government of Canada was prepared to take over the road on conditions that would be favourable to them, that moment the stock began to go up. The Minister says that on October 10 the stock was selling on the market at 66 or 65. The minister, I presume, is aware that there is an immensity of very good securities at all times selling on the market that bring a very much higher rate of interest than four per cent. No doubt he is also aware that call money and many other investments have been very high. I would ask him this question: If the railway still remained in the hands of the Grand Trunk, and there were no prospects of the Government coming to the rescue and taking it over, what wouldT be the condition of affairs? With their deficit for the last financial year which we have reason to believe exists- for although we have asked for a statement and cannot get it, we have reason to believe that the Grand Trunk Company for the year 1919 will have a deficit to show- if the road were still in the hands of the company with the possibility of that deficit, and with all kinds of security, gilt-edged and other kinds being offered, bearing twice the interest at which these securities are selling, I should like to know what the minister thinks the Grand Trunk stock would be worth to day.
, Mr. MEIGHEN: I might tell my hon. friend this, that before the agreement was entered into the common stock was. worth 9J; to-day it is worth 5i.
